Synthetic Silviculture: Growing a Forest, Forming a World

Nobody draws a forest. Trees grow by the light they can reach, shade one another and die, and the forest is what is left. This paper takes that machine apart, sets it beside everything else that grows forests and worlds today, and scores it against the laws real forests obey.

iori1

1Jorik Jonathan Chase, 3DIE — Design, Art & Technologies Label. Paper 0.3 of a series, a companion to paper 0. In preparation, November 2026.

The paper in one paragraph

Paper 0 grew a forest in the page, after Makowski and colleagues' Synthetic Silviculture, and set it on a 10 km landscape formed by rivers. This paper is about that forest. It explains the model one rule at a time. It sets the model beside the methods that came before it and the ones published since, each run live in the page where a page can run it. It scores the forest against the numbers foresters and ecologists have measured on real trees, as paper 0 scored the rivers against Earth's drainage laws. Measured on five seeds, the reduced model thins as crowded stands do. Mean tree mass falls with density at −1.65 to −1.92, near the foresters' −3/2. Stem mass grows as diameter to the power 3.0, where real trees give 2.89. Its trees branch a little less than real ones, and their box dimension sits at the low edge of laser-scanned trees. Its plot is too small to measure canopy gaps; a stand of individual trees on 16 ha (2.6) is not, and its gaps fall off as a power law of exponent 2.64 to 2.80, steeper than the Amazon's 1.66 to 2.50, as a forest with no storm or fire should. One correction to paper 0 follows: the forest law Makowski checked is the diameter form, not the mass form.

Written so far: chapter 1, the lineage (chapter 2) and the scorecard (chapter 4); the rest is planned below with its contents. Every figure starts when it scrolls into view; drag in the 3-D ones to orbit, and use pinch or ⌘/Alt with the wheel to zoom.

1. What Silviculture Means Here

Silviculture is the foresters' word for growing and tending forests. Makowski and colleagues took it for growing them in a computer [1].

A tree is a branching fractal, but its shape is not chosen. It is the record of a search. Every year each bud is lit or shaded. The light it gets is passed down to the trunk and handed back up as vigour, more to the well-lit branch and less to the shaded one, by the split Borchert and Honda measured on a tropical tree [2]. Vigorous buds grow, starved branches are shed, and the crown ends up filling the light it can reach. Pałubicki and colleagues grew single trees this way [3].

A forest is the same search with neighbours. Every plant shades the plants beneath it, so the light one tree takes is the light another loses. Grown trees scatter seeds around them, seeds take root only where light reaches the ground, and plants die of age or of shade. Makowski's model runs this at three scales: a module, a small group of branches that grows as one; a plant, a tree of modules; and the ecosystem, all the plants sharing one field of shadow. Nothing in the rules says forest. Pioneers come first, shade-tolerant trees take over beneath them, and the stand thins as it grows.

Paper 0 built a reduced version of that model in the page (§3.1) and set it on a landscape formed by uplift and rivers (§3.2). It is the series' clearest case of paper 0's claim: a rough world made by a process, not drawn. This paper asks three questions of it. Where does it come from, and what has been built since (chapters 2 and 3)? How close is it to real forests, measured rather than judged by eye (chapter 4)? What should it take from the state of the art next (chapter 5)?

2. The Lineage, Live

Five ways to grow a tree, from 1968 to paper 0, each run below. Every one adds a rule to the one before, and every one grows beside the same wall.

The wall is a test. It stands 3 m to one side of the seedling, 10 m tall and 10 m long, lower than a grown tree. A method that knows nothing of the world grows straight into it. A method that knows space keeps out of it. A method that knows light turns away from its shadow before it ever touches it. Under every figure the same instrument runs as the tree grows, the one chapter 4 uses: how many segments, how tall, Horton's branching ratio, the box dimension, the crown's lean (the mean position of its leaves across the wall's axis; negative is away from the wall), and how many segments sit inside the wall, drawn orange. All five start from seed 1; the button gives the next seed, and the wall can be taken away.

2.1 Rewriting: the L-System

Lindenmayer wrote down how a filament of algae grows as a rule that rewrites every cell at once [4]. Read the symbols as the moves of a pen in space, a turtle that draws, turns and returns to a saved position, and the same rewriting draws plants [5]. The tree below is the book's monopodial tree, after Honda's model of branching [6]: a trunk that sends side shoots 0.6 times its length, each side shoot forking left and right in a plane, all of it rewritten at every step.

It is exact and instant, a thousand segments in under a millisecond, and it is the same tree whatever the seed. It is also blind: 65 of its segments grow inside the wall, with or without the wall there, because the rule never reads the world. Its branching is perfectly binary, so Horton's ratio is exactly 2, half the 3.6 to 4.8 of real trees, and its widths shrink by 0.707 at every fork so Leonardo's rule holds by construction. Its box dimension is 1.40.

2.2 Competing for Space: Space Colonisation

Runions, Lane and Prusinkiewicz turned the problem inside out [7]. Scatter points through the volume the crown will fill. Every point pulls the nearest branch tip within reach; every pulled tip grows one step toward the points that chose it; a point a branch reaches is used up. Two branches cannot grow into the same space, because a point serves one branch. The rule knows one thing about the world, which space is free, and that is enough to keep it out of the wall: points are never made inside it, and no branch may grow there.

Without the wall the crown fills the whole ellipsoid and 139 to 158 segments stand where the wall would be. With it, none do (one, on one seed), and the crown leans 0.1 to 0.2 m away. The tree looks right because it fills its envelope: Horton's ratio is 4.2 to 4.5, inside the real range, and the box dimension 1.52 to 1.54, that of a laser-scanned ash. But the envelope is drawn, not grown, and the method knows nothing of light. A branch in the wall's shadow grows as well as one in the sun.

2.3 Competing for Light: the Self-Organising Tree

Pałubicki and colleagues let light decide [3]. Every bud casts a pyramid of shade on the space below it, and reads its own light from the shade cast by everything above. The light of all the buds is summed down to the trunk and handed back up as vigour, split at every fork between the continuing axis and the side branch in proportion to the light each side gathered, weighted by λ, the apical control of Borchert and Honda [2]. A bud with vigour v grows ⌊v⌋ new internodes toward its default direction, bent toward the light and upward. A side branch that gathers too little light for its size is shed. The wall here is opaque: it casts shade like a crown and nothing is lit inside it.

The tree now answers the wall without touching it: no segment inside it, and a crown that leans 0.76 to 0.89 m away, against 0.19 to 0.60 m with no wall on the same seeds. Nothing tells the tree where the wall is; the branches on that side are shaded, gather less light, get less vigour and are shed. Its numbers are the closest to real trees of the five: Horton's ratio 3.1 to 3.3, box dimension 1.52 to 1.55. Two of its constants are ours, and they matter. With the light constant C at 1, every side bud is shaded to nothing by the buds above it and the tree grows as a bare pole; at 2 it branches. The internodes keep one length here, where the paper lets them stretch to twice that, which doubled the leader's growth.

2.4 Modules: Paper 0's Tree

Makowski and colleagues kept the light and the vigour and changed the unit [1]. A tree is built from modules, small pre-shaped groups of branches that grow as one, chosen from nine shapes by how strongly the axis dominates and how vigorous the parent is. Light comes from how much a module's bounding sphere overlaps its neighbours' and from a shadow grid shared by every plant. A tree of a hundred years is a few thousand segments, cheap enough for a forest. This is paper 0's simulator, unchanged; the wall is written into its shadow grid as opaque cells.

It grows the tallest tree of the five, 23 to 28 m in 120 years, with Horton's ratio 3.6 to 3.8, just inside the real range. It responds least to the wall: the crown's lean is −0.43 to 0.07 m with the wall and −0.51 to 0.24 m without. An open-grown tree of this model is narrow, the sparse crown chapter 4 measured as a low box dimension (1.28 to 1.40), and it mostly grows past the wall's top, where the light is. Modules were made for forests, not for one tree beside a wall.

2.5 Neighbours That Grow: the Ecosystem

The last rule is that the neighbours are alive. Trees scatter seeds; a seed takes root only where enough light reaches the ground; plants die of age or of starvation. The wall stays, but now it stands in a forest, and it matters less than the trees.

Here the wall stops mattering. After 200 years on three seeds, the trees within 6 m of the wall's near side average 4.7, 29.7 and 12.5 m with the wall and 5.9, 23.4 and 16.2 m without it; the rest of the plot averages 9.9 to 12.7 m either way. What stands beside the wall depends on which trees happened to take root there and what shades them, far more than on the wall. A forest is its own neighbour. This is the scale paper 0 built the model for, and the one chapter 4 scores: about 5 ms a year for 250 to 340 plants.

2.6 A Hectare of Light: Stamps

The last five figures grew one tree, then a forest of 0.1 ha. Forests are measured over hectares, and some of their laws only show there. Canopy gaps follow a power law, but the fit counts gaps from 20 m² to a hectare [8] [9], and chapter 4 could not measure it on 32 m. iLand, the forest model that runs ten thousand hectares tree by tree, gets there by dropping the branches [10]. A tree is a stem diameter, a height and a crown; its shade is a stamp, a fixed pattern it presses onto a 2 m grid of light. Here the trees are stamped tallest first: each reads the light left over its crown by every taller tree, then presses its own shade in. One stamp per tree a year, and a hectare costs about a millisecond.

The stand settles where real temperate forests stand: about 570 stems of 5 cm or more per hectare, a basal area of 43 m² per hectare, 155 to 169 trees thicker than 30 cm, a canopy 32 m tall with 1.6 to 2.8 % of the ground under a hole. On one hectare there are one to three gaps big enough to count, and no exponent. On sixteen there are 39 to 49, and the exponent is 2.64 to 2.80 (± 0.25 to 0.29) over three seeds. The Amazon's runs from 1.66 to 2.50, and above 2 means a forest whose gaps are made by single trees falling, not by storms or fire [9]. This forest has no storms and no fire, and its exponent says so: too many small gaps, too few large ones. The pioneer, which needs a large gap to take root, dies out within a century, as it does in paper 0's plot. The stamp, the growth curves and every rate here are ours, listed in the code; iLand's own stamps come from a model of the sun's path through a crown, ours are a Gaussian under a vertical sun.

2.7 The Air Under the Canopy

A forest makes its own weather. Pałubicki and colleagues coupled their forests to the water in the soil, the evaporation from leaves, clouds and rain [11]. The smallest piece of that is the shade's coolness. Measured at about a hundred sites, the warmest days are about 4 °C cooler under a forest canopy than in the open, and the hotter the day the larger the difference [12]. Here the cooling of each 2 m cell is 4 °C times its canopy cover, scaled with the heat of the day, and one consequence follows: the shade-tolerant tree's seedlings only take root where the air stays below 31 °C.

Measured on 4 ha over 300 years and three seeds, the canopy cools the air under it by 3.1 °C on a warmest day of 26 °C and by 4.7 °C on one of 34 °C, the range De Frenne and colleagues report. Up to 34 °C the shade keeps the whole floor below the tolerant tree's limit, and the forest is the one of 2.6: 536 to 600 tolerant stems per hectare and no pioneers. At 38 °C the shade is no longer enough, every cell is above 31 °C, no tolerant seedling takes root, and within 300 years the forest is 659 to 689 pioneers per hectare, every tolerant tree gone. The switch is sudden because our threshold is a single number; a real species' response to heat is a curve, and the forest would pass through a mixture. What the figure shows is the loop that Ecoclimates simulates in full: the canopy makes the climate its own seedlings need, and above some heat it cannot.

2.8 Fire: Ground, Ladder, Crown

Fire in Paradise burned forests grown by Makowski's simulator, module by module, coupled to the air that the fire heats [13]; Scintilla added what burns on the ground, grass, litter and duff, and the move from ground to crown [14]. The rule foresters use for that move is old: a surface fire starts a crown fire when it is intense enough to reach the crown's base [15]. Small trees under the canopy are the ladder. Here each 2 m cell holds three fuels: ground fuel (litter under crowns, grass where the ground is lit), ladder fuel (small trees whose crowns reach down near the ground) and crown fuel (the canopy). A ground fire spreads by its fuel and the wind, climbs where the ladder reaches a canopy, and a crown fire runs through the canopy, faster and further downwind.

The fire was lit on the upwind edge of 4 ha at 200 years, three seeds, three winds, with and without the ladder. It is a threshold, as fire on a grid of fuels is: most fires in light or moderate wind went out within a few cells (0 to 12 % of the plot burnt), and most in strong wind burnt 71 to 77 %. With the ladder in place, the two strong-wind fires that ran climbed into the canopy and 20 to 21 % of the plot burnt as crown fire, killing about half the trees (2034 of 4196, 2146 of 4323). With the ladder cleared, not one of the nine fires reached a crown. The ground fire still ran as far, through the grass that grows where the ground is lit, but it killed small trees and left the canopy standing. That is Van Wagner's point and the reason for thinning: the crown fire is cut off by removing what it climbs. What the fire did not do is bring the pioneer back. Sixty years after each fire there were still no pioneers in the plot, because none were left to seed it; paper 0's plot brings seed in from outside, this one does not. The fuels, their loads and every rate are ours. Fire in Paradise and Scintilla solve the heat, the air and the combustion of each branch; this figure keeps only who catches from whom.

2.9 Roots and the Root Plate

Half a tree is underground. Rhizomorph grew roots with the same vigour logic as shoots, in a soil of water and texture, and found that the familiar root types, a tap root, a heart, a flat plate of laterals, follow from the soil rather than being chosen [16]. Here the shoot is the self-organising tree of 2.3 at fifteen years, and the roots grow by space colonisation (2.2) toward points of soil water. The soil decides where the water is: deep in sand, nowhere below 0.7 m on rock, above a water table at 1 m in wet clay. The roots get one segment for every leaf cluster of the shoot, a crude balance between what the tree gathers above and below. Then a storm.

The same three trees, grown in each soil, spend the same root length, 125 to 153 m against 383 to 477 m of shoot, because we set the budget; where it goes is the soil's doing. In deep sand the roots go down to 3.8 to 4.0 m and the plate is narrow, 2.4 to 2.5 m in radius and 1.1 m deep. On rock they stop at 0.7 m and spread, a plate of 3.4 to 3.6 m and half a metre deep; in wet clay, 1 m and 3.3 to 3.5 m. A tap root and a flat plate come out of the same rule, as Rhizomorph found. The pit the storm leaves holds 6.4 to 8.4 m³ in every soil, a deep bowl in sand and a wide saucer on rock. Paper 0's forest throws trees into pits and mounds of one size; here the root system would choose it. The hinge, the plate's 80 % share and the half-ellipsoid pit are ours.

2.10 Learned Trees

Since 2024 trees have also been generated the way text is, a token at a time. Lee and colleagues trained a transformer on 155,000 L-system strings [17]; Wang and colleagues wrote a tree as a sequence of branch tokens, depth first, and trained a 79-million-parameter model on trees grown by Rhizomorph's simulator [18]. The second fact matters more than the first: the learned generators learn from procedural ones. Neither model runs in a page. The smallest model of the same kind does: an n-gram, which counts which token followed every run of the last n − 1, and writes by drawing from those counts. Here it learns from eight self-organising trees grown beside the wall, written as tokens the way Wang and colleagues write them.

The eight teachers are 15 m tall, with 1049 to 1491 segments, a Horton ratio of 2.60 to 3.22, a box dimension of 1.44 to 1.52, and every one leans away from the wall (−0.31 to −0.99 m) without a segment in it. Samples of order 6, three seeds, are 28 to 46 m tall, with a Horton ratio of 2.8 to 3.4 and a box dimension of 1.35 to 1.39; their lean is −2.3 to 3.8 m, either way, and two of the three grow into the wall, 49 and 251 segments in it. Order 1 and 3 do worse and order 10 no better: 45 to 125 m tall. The n-gram learns how a branch turns and forks, the local grammar, and none of what holds a tree together: where to stop, how tall to be, which side the light is on. Nothing in a token says where in space the tree is, so the wall cannot be learned from tokens at all. The transformers of Lee and of Wang and colleagues see far more context than ten tokens, and their trees hold together; they are still taught by simulators, and the question this chapter asks of each method, does the tree answer its light, is one a model trained on trees in open ground has no way to answer.

3. The Ground, Live

In preparation. From the stream-power law to paper 0's 10 km region, and what learned world generators do instead.

  1. Uplift against stream power (Cordonnier and colleagues 2016), and its implicit solve.
  2. Paper 0's region: rivers, lakes, strata, climate, with its drainage statistics.
  3. Stochastic geomorphological transport at plot scale (McDonald and Cordonnier 2026), reduced.
  4. Learned terrain and world models (InfiniteDiffusion, Genie 3, Matrix-Game): what they do that a law-based world cannot yet, and what they do not measure.

4. The Scorecard

Rivers obey tight laws, and paper 0 scored its rivers against them. Forests obey laws too, looser ones. This chapter scores the forest the same way.

4.1 Self-Thinning, in Both Forms

Plant a stand densely and leave it. The trees grow, close their canopy and start to starve one another. From then on the stand loses stems as it gains wood, along a line that foresters found almost a century ago. It comes in two forms. Reineke counted stems per hectare against their quadratic mean diameter and found a slope of −1.605 on a log–log plot [19]. Yoda and colleagues plotted mean plant mass against density and found −3/2 [20]. Real stands scatter around both. In German stands measured since 1870, Reineke's slope runs from −1.42 for oak to −1.79 for beech [21]. Of 63 data sets, 20 differ significantly from −3/2, and the slope follows the species' shade tolerance [22].

Paper 0 said that Makowski's full model reproduces the −3/2 mass law. It does not say that. Makowski's figure plots density against trunk diameter, the Reineke form, and calls it the 3/2 law, after Zeide [1] [23]. Paper 0 also gave −2.3 to −3.1 for its own reduced model, in the mass form. The stands behind that number and its fitting window were not recorded, so here it is measured again under one stated rule. The rule: 576 seedlings of one species on a jittered grid over the 32 m plot (5,600 per hectare), no new seedlings, trees counted from 5 cm of stem diameter, and the slope fitted only after density has fallen 10 % below its peak. Every death in such a stand is a tree starved by shade.

Over five seeds the tolerant tree thins at −1.65 to −1.89 in mass and −1.93 to −2.16 in diameter. The pioneer thins at −1.84 to −1.92 in mass and −1.39 to −1.45 in diameter. Both mass slopes sit a little steeper than −3/2, inside the spread Weller found. The pioneer's diameter slope sits at oak's end of the measured range. The tolerant tree's is steeper than any species Pretzsch and Biber measured: it sheds more stems per centimetre of growth than a real stand does. The two forms are tied by how mass grows with diameter. Here stem mass grows as diameter to the power 2.96–3.04, against 2.89 (2.71–3.14) measured on real trees [24], so a steep diameter slope and a near −3/2 mass slope are the same fact.

4.2 The Table

The other statistics are measured on two kinds of run. The architecture comes from single trees grown alone in open light, the tolerant tree for 200 years and the pioneer for 45. The stand statistics come from the mixed forest of paper 0's figure (30 % tolerant) after 400 years. All five seeds are in each range. The script is tools/silviculture/measure.mjs; it runs the five seeds in about 25 s.

Sources for the right-hand column: allometry and Horton ratios from the tables collected by Eloy and colleagues [24]; the Leonardo ratio from Bentley and colleagues [25]; box dimensions of laser-scanned ash, maple and beech, with boxes from 30 m down to 10 cm, from Seidel and colleagues [26]; stem sizes across 14 tropical plots from Muller-Landau and colleagues [27]; canopy gaps from airborne laser scans of the Amazon [8] [9]. The metabolic theory predicts θ = 2 for stem sizes [28]; the plots reject it in 13 of 14 forests.

How to read it. Mass against diameter, height against diameter and the mass form of self-thinning land in or next to the real ranges. They were not tuned to; they come out of the light and vigour rules. The trees branch a little less than real ones: fewer side branches per order (Rn below 3.6) and slightly thicker steps between orders. Their box dimension is lower, the sparse open-grown crown paper 0 already noted. Leonardo's rule is not a test here, because the pipe model writes it into the code: a parent's cross-section is the sum of its children's. Stem sizes are near the theory's 2 but rest on a few dozen stems, and the large stems fall off more gently than in real forests. Canopy gaps cannot be measured at all, because the fit counts gaps from 20 m² up to a hectare and the plot is a tenth of a hectare.

The mathematics

Self-thinning: least squares on log10, after density N (stems ≥ 5 cm per hectare) first falls below 0.9·max N. Reineke: log N against log Dq, with Dq = √(mean D²). Yoda: log m̄ against log N, with m̄ the mean woody mass (pipe-model volume × 600 kg/m³).

Horton: Strahler order on the tree's segments (a tip is order 1; a segment takes the largest order among its children, plus one if two children share it); a stream is a maximal chain of one order. Rn = 10−s for the slope s of log10(number of streams) against order, Rd and Rl likewise from the streams' mean base diameter and mean length.

Box dimension: points every 2 cm along every segment, boxes from 10 cm to half the tree's extent in steps of 1.4, the slope of log(boxes hit) against −log(box size).

Stem sizes: the continuous power-law maximum-likelihood estimate θ = 1 + n / Σ ln(Di/Dmin), standard error (θ − 1)/√n [29].

5. What the Forest Takes Next

In preparation. The state of the art, ranked by what it would add per unit of work.

  1. A plot of a hectare or more, shaded by light stamps on a 2 m grid as iLand does, so canopy gaps and forest edges can be measured.
  2. Leonardo's exponent as a species parameter, so the area ratio becomes a measurement rather than a rule.
  3. A microclimate field under the canopy, feeding the decay of logs and where seedlings take root.
  4. Root plates grown from a root graph on uprooted trees.
  5. Fire moving from ground to ladder to crown fuel.
  6. The simulator's own modules drawn at landscape scale, with GPU level of detail.
  7. On the ground: the drainage harness run on real Earth tiles and on other generators, the first such scoreboard across families.
